body: The pipes go first: the far shower working its way toward hot, one knock and a long pause and two more, and under them the rain on the window toward the Grove, steady since Monday night. Jack got to sleep a little after five, on top of the blanket in his clothes, with the RAZR rising and falling on his chest. The light at the blind is gray and has no source.
The knock on the door isn’t Kevin’s. Kevin knocks twice, politely, and says his own name. This is three, flat, and nothing after it.

Theo is already up, which Theo is not before ten without a court order. He’s at the desk in the wine-colored robe with the Sigma Rho pin on the blotter and Hollis on the nightstand in his cup, and he gets to the door first.

Laney is in the doorway with no face on. That’s the first thing, and then it’s the freckles: across the bridge of her nose and out over both cheekbones, copper on porcelain, hundreds of them, and Jack, up on one elbow with the crease of the blanket still in his cheek, has known her since August and has never seen a single one. Her hand comes up flat over her nose and the near cheek, and stays there, and comes down again. It’s no use, and she seems to know it. Her hair is in a rubber band. She holds her phone in both hands at her breastbone, the way she held the root beer at Sully’s before she set it down without drinking.
She looks at Jack once. There’s no ice in it and no “Night.” Then she looks at Theo.
“Theodore. Hall.”

Theo, who has an opinion on every doorway he has ever stood in, has none. He starts, “Give me a second to —” and she says, “No,” and he lifts Hollis off the nightstand in both hands and goes out barefoot in the robe, with the teacup held in front of him at the level of his heart.
It is the first time since the Sunday of the status that Laney Price has come looking for Theo. Since then she has addressed him by text in the third person and, at Sully’s, in the imperative.

The door shuts behind them. Jack doesn’t get up to listen; there would be nothing to hear. The hall carpet takes whatever’s said, and what’s left is the pipes, knocking along the wall toward the far shower. On the nightstand a pale ring marks where the cup has sat all week.
He sits on the edge of the bed with one boot on and the other in his hand. The rain goes on. Ten minutes by the RAZR.

Theo comes back alone, with Hollis, and shuts the door with his heel. He sets the cup down in its ring and dresses without a word, and Jack has not seen this before: Theo narrates a cuff link. Now he ties the tie, undoes it, ties it again. He puts the Rolex on over the wrong sleeve and moves it. To free both hands for the cuffs he hangs his umbrella by its crook from the post of Jack’s bed, and then the cup is back in his palms, level, and he’s at the door with his back to the room.
“Costigan.” Too casual. “Where are you at eleven?”
“Tonight?” Jack says. “Here. I owe Hale three pages.”
“Here,” Theo says, and nods twice, like a man confirming a reservation. “Hollis likes to know where everyone is. He keeps a ledger. It’s mostly dining hall hours.”

He goes. It is another minute before Jack sees the umbrella still hanging from his bedpost, black and enormous, dripping onto the blanket. Theo, who held it over the cup on Sunday and not over himself, has gone out into Wednesday’s rain with the cup and without it.

Jack is pulling on the second boot when he sees his desk chair. His clothes are on it: yesterday’s flannel, the gray Mooney hoodie, the jeans, three undershirts and the socks, folded in thirds with the edges lined up. They were in the third dryer in the basement, damp and warm, when he left the laundry room, and he hasn’t been down since. He picks up the flannel. It smells of the basement, sweet and chemical, and of warm lint.
Every pair of socks is paired. Jack Costigan has never in his life paired a sock.

s13.slug: WEDNESDAY · 10:50 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE 4TH-FLOOR LOUNGE — MEETING #2
body: The lounge door is propped open on its wedge, and the fluorescents come out through the gap and lay a white stripe down the hall carpet, the only lit thing on the floor. On the stairwell door behind him Priya’s laminate still has the pen underneath it: WEDGES ARE A LIFESTYLE. He has come up for hot water. The tap is in the vending alcove just inside the lounge door, the instant coffee is in the Carhartt, and Hale’s three pages are due at one tomorrow with a title and nothing else. His jeans have not forgiven the rain.

He opens the door the rest of the way with his foot. Inside, a hand slaps the frame of the whiteboard and the board goes over on its swivel, end over end, a good deal faster than the swivel was built for: a white blur, a squeal of casters, and at the top of the turn, for half a second, upside down, the back of it goes past with a word on it in pink capitals, FACTS, underlined three times, the last line running off the edge. Then the other side comes round and rocks to a stop. USEFUL IDIOTS FOR CHRISTIAN NATIONALISM, and under it COSTIGAN | BROUSSARD in Margot’s marks, months old. The side he knows.

Theo has one hand on the frame and the other in his blazer pocket. Laney is on the window seat with her knees up and a pink marker in her fist, her face back on, lashes and lip, the copper hair brushed to a shine. Margot is in the armchair with a notebook open on her knee. Kevin is on the couch in plaid pajama pants and a quarter-zip, bolt upright, arms crossed, with the posture of a hostage who has read his rights. On the coffee table, on a coaster, Hollis presides from his teacup.

Jack has seen these four in this room a hundred nights. He has never seen them sit up straight. And Laney and Theo are sharing a room with no third party to address each other through, which hasn’t happened in ten days.
“Costigan.” Theo’s voice is a half-step too warm, and the board is still rocking behind him. “Perfect timing. You’ve caught us.”
“Did the board just —”
“It’s on a swivel,” says Theo.
“It’s an excellent swivel,” says Margot, from behind the notebook.

“We’re planning Delaney’s nineteenth.” Theo is not going to stop now. “Valentine’s Day, which falls on a Sunday this year, a gift, because there’s no class on Sundays and everyone is already feeling a little bad about their lives. Agenda.” He holds up three fingers. “The cake, from the Vons on Mission, her name spelled correctly in writing. The guest list, fourteen, a crowd. And a theme.”
“Teal is a hostage situation,” Laney says from the window seat.
“Teal has been withdrawn.”

“I want real piping on the cake,” Laney says. “Not gel. Gel is for people who’ve given up. And I’m being surprised.” She does the face: hands to both cheeks, eyes wide, mouth a perfect O, held, and dropped like a window shade. “I’ve been practicing.”
“She is being surprised in committee,” says Margot.
“And Hollis,” Laney says. “On the guest list.”
“Hollis is staff.”
“Hollis is a *guest*, Theodore.”
“Hollis has abstained,” Theo says. “He’s an egg of principle.”
“I’d like it entered that I want a tiara,” says Laney. “A small one. Plastic. I’ll know.”
“The tiara is in the minutes.”
“The tiara is not in the minutes,” says Margot.
“It’s in the minutes,” says Theo. “In pencil.”
“Overlord took two years,” he adds, to Jack. “The beaches didn’t even have a theme.”
“That’s a lot of work for a sheet cake,” Jack says.
“It’s a very complicated sheet cake.”
“Sixty dollars,” Theo goes on. “Margot has proposed we spend all of it on a banner.”
“Banners are the oldest instrument of coercion,” Margot says. “I am on record against them. We are getting a banner.”
“Kev,” Jack says. “You okay?”

“I want it noted that I’m here under protest.” Kevin says it to the room at large, fast. “I was in bed. I have a quiz at eight a.m., I was in my bed with my quiz, and I was brought here, I was physically brought, and I think as a general principle that everybody should leave everybody alone.”
“Noted, sugar,” says Laney.
“I’m not on the committee,” Kevin tells Jack. “I’m the designated adult. Nobody asked.”
“Want me to say you’re excused?”
“There’s no mechanism,” Kevin says. “I checked.”
“What’s the notebook?” Jack says to Margot.
“Participant observation. I’m told it’s legitimate.”
“Of what?”
“That is what the notebook is for.”
“Theodore,” Laney says, to the room, “tell him the tap sticks.”
“The tap sticks, Costigan.”
“I heard her, Theo.”
“Tell him I know,” says Laney.
“Indirect discourse,” says Margot. “It’s in the literature.”
He gets his mug under the tap. The water begins, thread by thread, to fill it. Behind him four people and an egg go quiet in the manner of people pretending to have been in the middle of something.

choices.text: “Put me down for the theme. Pageant.”
response: Laney’s mouth goes, and comes back, and goes again, like a car trying to start in January. She looks hard at the ceiling and overrules it.
“Pageant,” Theo says, writing nothing down. “A theme with legs.”
“Seconded,” says Margot. “For the data. The motion carries over my objection.”
“Please don’t second anything,” Kevin says. Then, fast: “If there’s a theme, I’d like it calm. Tide pools.”
“Tide pools are a subcommittee,” says Theo. He turns to the window seat. “Delaney, you’ll need to leave the room for the vote.”
“I’m *in* the room, Theodore. I’m being surprised in it.”

Laney unfolds from the window seat and crosses to the door, and because the tap is beside the door, he’s in her way. She doesn’t go around. Her hand closes on his left arm above the elbow and squeezes, hard and quick, and lets go. “Night,” she says to the hall.
Kevin examines the ceiling tiles. Margot’s pen comes down on the page and goes up again without having written anything.
“We’ve reconciled,” Theo says. “Over a principle.”
“Several,” says Laney.
“Name one.”
“The principle,” Theo says, “is that you don’t ask the committee what the committee is for.”
“I asked,” Kevin tells Jack. “They said it was a committee thing.”
“It was a long negotiation,” says Margot. “I took minutes.”

Laney is already up. She crosses to the door, and the tap is beside the door, and he is in her way; her hand closes on his right arm above the elbow, quick and hard, and lets go. “Night,” she says, to the hall, as if she had been saying it all along.
Kevin looks at the ceiling. Margot’s pen writes a letter, stops, and lays itself along the spine of the notebook.

The tap gives him water at the speed of the Delgado plumbing, a thread, a drip, a thread, and the room waits him out in total silence. Theo’s hand stays on the frame of a board that has stopped rocking. Kevin studies the ceiling tiles above the couch. Margot’s pen hovers over the notebook, and hovers, and the page stays blank. On the coffee table Hollis watches with the serenity of the unhatched. Once, Theo opens his mouth, and Laney says, “Don’t,” without turning her head, and he closes it.

About halfway, Laney gets up off the window seat and crosses to the door, and has to stand there at his elbow, because the tap is next to the door and he is next to the tap. She waits. The mug fills a third of the way and stops. Starts. He puts in the coffee and stirs it with the wrong end of a pen.
When it’s full, she goes first. Her hand closes on his arm above the elbow, quick and hard, and lets go. “Night,” she says, and the hall carpet takes her flats.
He follows her out with the mug. At the door he looks back at the couch. “You’ll live, Kev.”
“That’s what they say to the ones who don’t,” says Kevin, to the ceiling. “I’d like it noted that this was worse than the quiz.”

s17.slug: THURSDAY · 3:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE LOBBY — THE REHEARSAL
body: The lobby smells of wet nylon and newsprint. The big storm has driven everyone indoors at once, and forty umbrellas lie open on the tile along the radiators to drain, black and navy and one plaid, a flock come in out of the weather. On the table by the mailboxes, tied in twine and still damp from the courier’s bag, sits a stack of Thursday’s *Tide*.
Jack takes one off the top. He knows what’s in it; he’s in it. He reads it standing at the mailboxes with the storm leaning on the glass doors behind him.

body.title: The Tide — FRONT STAGE · by Margot Lindqvist
body.text: “There is no backstage,” Skye Callender told me, over pie, in a diner on the wharf. “There are just more stages.” Erving Goffman would call that a very backstage thing to say. Callender counts four selves on a weekday — five on Thursdays — and says her boyfriend is “the only person I’ve ever met who’s the same in every room.” Of his faith: “I believe *he* does. Those are different, and the second one is very attractive.” Asked to respond, the subject’s boyfriend described himself as “load-bearing.” I did not write it down. I did not need to.

body.text: “There is no backstage,” Skye Callender told me, over pie, in a diner on the wharf. “There are just more stages.” Erving Goffman would call that a very backstage thing to say. Callender counts four selves on a weekday — five on Thursdays — and says her boyfriend is “the only person I’ve ever met who’s the same in every room.” Of his faith: “I believe *he* does. Those are different, and the second one is very attractive.” Asked to respond, the subject’s boyfriend said, “She’s right.” I have chosen to treat this as data.

body.text: “There is no backstage,” Skye Callender told me, over pie, in a diner on the wharf. “There are just more stages.” Erving Goffman would call that a very backstage thing to say. Callender counts four selves on a weekday — five on Thursdays — and says her boyfriend is “the only person I’ve ever met who’s the same in every room.” Of his faith: “I believe *he* does. Those are different, and the second one is very attractive.” Asked to respond, the subject’s boyfriend said, “No comment” — a comment.

body: He thumbs the RAZR on. It has been off since one o’clock, in the Carhartt, at Hale’s table, and it chirps, and keeps chirping, and he goes past all of it to Margot’s name.

At the far end of the mailboxes, Theo and Laney have arranged themselves, shoulders turned half toward each other and half toward the lobby, one hand each raised to chest height as if weighing something. They are speaking at the volume of people who would like to be heard in the back row.
“— and that’s why it’s so important, Theodore,” Laney is saying, to the middle of the room, “to have *all the facts* before you assume anything about anybody.”
“I couldn’t agree more, Delaney.” Theo lifts a finger. “*Communication.* It’s the bedrock.”

Then they see him. Both freeze mid-gesture, Theo’s finger up, Laney’s palm out flat in the air as if smoothing a very large tablecloth. They hold it until the radiator ticks twice. Then they go on, louder and worse.
“Which is *exactly* what I was saying,” Laney says.
“*Exactly,*” says Theo, louder still.
“Are you two okay?” Jack says.
“Never better,” says Theo.

Laney crosses to Jack in four brisk steps, holding out her umbrella: pink, a scalloped edge, a brass handle. “Take it.” She presses the handle into his hand, and it’s warm from hers. Then she turns on her heel, chin up, and says to nobody in particular, at a volume that reaches the street: “I’ll want that *back*.”
The stairwell door opens, and Lena comes through the lobby with her mailbox key held out in front of her and a folder under one arm. She has the gray cardigan on.
Theo turns from Laney and gives her a nod, a good one, exact, with the correct number of degrees, and a flat “Broussard.”
“Theo,” Lena says, and keeps going.

At her mailbox she turns the key and takes out a catalog and one envelope, shuts the little door and locks it, and that is the entire transaction. She does not look at Jack. He has turned to his own box, with his key in it and the little door open on nothing, and he stays turned that way until her step has gone back up the stairs.
Jack has watched Theo be charming to Lena for five months. He has never watched him be correct.
Behind him there is a small, wounded noise. Theo has his eyes shut. “Too many degrees.”
“Not a one,” Laney whispers, lit up like a marquee. “Perfect.”
“Dude.” Doug is on the bench by the radiators with his laptop on his knees and his socks steaming on the grate. “I’m doing the wall. As a public service.” He turns the screen so the lobby can see it.

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it. Alarm Five: twenty-seven days; she’d said twenty-six. Out past one, four nights of six — she doesn’t sleep, she counts. Not writing it down. Sunday: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS. Nineteen on the solstice, four days early, under protest. Likes us. On the record. Lit a candle for research. Took Skye’s side about the rose. Goffman, 1956. Wrote TED in her notebook and underlined it. Gave to Partners In Health and sent the rest of us there — Farmer’s Catholic, sort of. Commented ‘Front stage.’ on my status. Wednesday night in the lounge, while Laney kept it short with Theo: keeping score. A page in her notebook says SKYE. Thursday at the Anchor she interviewed Skye for her column. She hated that it was good. Her column ran Thursday: ‘Front Stage.’ It’s good. I told her twice.

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’ Ma wrote her. Three days after Christmas. Pittsburgh’s cheaper than Cleveland. She looked. Wednesday, in Eli’s truck, I told her. She said she did everything right, and she did. ‘It just isn’t the thing, is it.’ She asked me to leave it up on Facebook till she’s told her mom at the table. Thursday at two she texted. Still praying for me — not a girlfriend thing, she says. At the twelve-ten she turned around across the aisle at the sign of peace and held out her hand. Then she held it out to Lena. At the airport, a week to the day: St. Raphael, for Nonna. Father Osei read the name at the twelve-ten, and she heard. Thanksgiving: told her mom at the table. Texted me first — happy Thanksgiving, praying for Nonna, taking it down now. Then she did. The Immaculate Conception, on the steps after the 12:10: white elephant, ten dollars, nothing that eats. Thomas is going home to Idaho in a Tupperware to see snow. The Advent party: ran the white elephant like a cattle auction. Three steals and it’s frozen. Her Christmas card found me in the lobby on finals Monday — six true facts about hermit crabs; number six, they need a friend. She sent my family one too, praying for Nonna’s hand, and Ma stood it at the front of the mantel. Christmas Eve she wrote on my Wall. The first day back, on the steps of St. Brendan’s, she said she saw, and she’s happy for me. Over Christmas she prayed I’d be happy. Thomas saw snow. At the Haiti table: her grandmother prayed that rosary at the gate of the Sunshine Mine in 1972, eight days. On the eighth day two men came up. She lent Skye her apron. Skye wrote her a letter, on paper. It came on St. Agnes, with a surfboard drawn on the back.

s19.slug: THURSDAY · 11:34 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE 4TH-FLOOR HALL — KEVIN
body: Past eleven the fourth-floor hall runs on its night lights, one amber bulb in four, and the lounge, for once, is dark. The carpet is wet in two tracks from the stairwell door. Kevin is outside 420 in plaid pajama pants and the quarter-zip, with his BlackBerry held in both hands at belt height, looking down the hall at that door, and when it opens and it’s Jack, with the fryer from the Anchor in his clothes and the curb still on his mouth, he starts talking before it has finished moving.

“Hey. Jack. Hi. I was going to knock on 412, but Theo’s got the egg, and the egg’s a light sleeper, and I didn’t want to be the person who — so I waited out here, which I realize is strange, it’s been maybe ten minutes, Doug’s asleep, Doug sleeps like a — okay.” He takes a breath that doesn’t seem to get all the way in. “I rehearsed this. I want you to know I rehearsed this. Margot says that’s a mistake.”
“How long was the rehearsal?” Jack says.
“Four minutes. In the shower.”
“How did it go?”

“It went great. It was a different conversation.” He thumbs the dark trackball. “The Walk for Life is Saturday. San Francisco. The Newman van leaves at five a.m. — five, a.m., I know — and it gets back around midnight if nobody gets lost, and somebody always gets lost. Six hours each way. Clare’s going. Her brothers are probably going, all four, it’s a pro-life march in San Francisco, half the Bay Area is going, her brothers are a subset.” The pause that follows is the first one he’s taken. “I’d like you to come. For me.”

Kevin organizes. In five months Jack has watched him organize a beach cleanup, a carpool, and two flats of water for a Haiti table, and every time it was *we*: the group is going, somebody should, we’re all signing up. He has never heard Kevin ask for something with an I in it.
“Do you need a buffer?” Jack says. “For the brothers?”
“I need somebody who’ll lie about it afterward. She said she’d love for me to meet them, and I said great, and then I went and looked up the fastest way to Canada.”
“Is Lena going?” Jack says.
“It’s a Newman thing,” says Kevin, fast.

Kevin, who answers a yes-or-no question with a yes or a no and a related fact about the human body, has answered with a category. Jack knows what it means. Six hours each way is twelve in one van, with no door to leave by.
“That’s not why I asked,” Kevin says, quieter, and it’s the slowest thing he’s said all night. The BlackBerry’s screen has gone dark in his hands. He doesn’t look at it.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something. Back from San Jose. His mother has a girl from their parish she wants him to call. Clare. She plays the violin in the Mass band. Wednesday he brought two flats of water to the Haiti table, which nobody asked for, and stayed to hold Clare’s violin case. ‘My mother knows your mother.’ Thursday he called Clare. His mother had the number, and his grandmother was on the speaker. She said yes to Sully’s. MLK Day he brought gloves for everybody. Tuesday in the basement he read us the first reading off his BlackBerry. Clare’s going to the Walk for Life, and so is he. He asked me to come — for him. I said yes.

choices.key: Kevin asked you onto the Walk for Life van, for him. You said yes. For him.
response: The speed goes out of Kevin all at once. For a moment he is only a pre-med in pajama pants in a hall. “Okay,” he says. “Okay. Thank you.”

Then, because he is Kevin, it comes back in under a breath: “Bring a coat, bring a sandwich, don’t bring a sign unless you want to hold a sign for six hours — Clare says they’re heavier than they look — and gloves, I have gloves —” and he’s backing through the door of 420 with the BlackBerry held against his chest, and from inside the dark, Doug, asleep, says, “Dude.”

choices.text: “Five a.m. You owe me a Clare.”
choices.key: Kevin asked you onto the Walk for Life van. You said yes, and that he owes you a Clare.
response: “Done,” Kevin says. “Payable in gloves, net thirty.” He laughs, a short surprised one, and covers his eyes with the heel of the hand that has the BlackBerry in it. “I can’t believe I said it out loud. *I’d like you to come.* I sound like a wedding invitation.”
“You sound like a person.”
“I’ll work on it.” He points the BlackBerry at Jack. “You’re on the list.”
“What list?”
“There’s always a list.” And he eases the door of 420 open on a roommate who, from the sound of it, could not be woken by the Walk itself.

choices.key: Kevin asked you onto the Walk for Life van. You said yes.
response: “Thank you,” Kevin says. “Respectfully.”
It doesn’t follow, and he knows it doesn’t, and his ears go red in the amber light. “I don’t know why I said that.”
“It’s fine.”
“It’s five a.m.”
“I heard.”
“Oh-five-hundred,” Kevin says, as if that helps. He backs up to the door of 420 and finds the knob behind him on the second try.
